title: Balanced Scorecard & Entity Segment Reporting (CMA P1-C · feeds BAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — side by side, never silently combined

Illustrative control totals: MBG's GL was $12,480,000.00 and Riverton's $16,920,000.00; MBG WIP was $14,480,000.00 and Riverton WIP $11,360,000.00. Both entities can appear on one management dashboard, but their bank accounts, ledgers, risks, and legal obligations remain separate. A consolidated view requires explicit eliminations, not silent addition.

The balanced scorecard translates strategy into linked financial and nonfinancial objectives. Segment reporting evaluates meaningful business components. Together they prevent management from judging performance through a single short-term profit number.

Balanced scorecard perspectives

  1. Financial: profitability, cash, working capital, return, leverage, and surety capacity.
  2. Customer/stakeholder: satisfaction, repeat work, claims, quality, schedule, and owner relationships.
  3. Internal process: estimating, procurement, project execution, billing, close, safety, and control.
  4. Learning and growth: people, skills, systems, data, culture, and improvement capacity.

The perspectives form a strategy hypothesis. Training and data quality can improve estimating and project reviews; better processes can improve schedule and customer outcomes; those can improve margin and cash. Measures must test the logic rather than decorate a dashboard.

Design measures correctly

Each measure needs definition, purpose, owner, source, frequency, target, threshold, and action. Pair lagging outcomes with leading drivers. Gross margin is lagging; estimate-to-complete update timeliness is leading. Cash is lagging; billing package cycle time is a driver.

Balance quantity, quality, time, cost, and risk. A target for faster invoice processing can cause duplicate or misclassified payments unless quality controls remain. A target for maximum utilization can create burnout, safety risk, or deferred maintenance.

Avoid vanity metrics and denominator manipulation. “90% on time” requires a defined milestone population and rules for scope changes. Preserve historical definitions or clearly restate trends.

Worked scorecard

The following targets are illustrative:

PerspectiveMeasureTargetGuardrail
FinancialForecast gross marginAt least 18%No unresolved WIP reconciliation
CustomerMilestones on scheduleAt least 90%Approved scope baseline
ProcessCost-to-complete updates100% by day 3Operations and finance approval
Learning/controlKey reconciliations cross-trainedTwo trained ownersSegregated preparer/reviewer

Suppose illustratively 18 of 20 milestones are on time: 90%, target met. But two on-time milestones used unapproved scope reductions. The guardrail reveals that the headline percentage does not prove performance.

Segment and entity reporting

A management segment may be an entity, geography, service line, project type, or responsibility center. Define it based on how management allocates resources and assesses performance. External segment reporting follows applicable accounting guidance and may not match every internal view.

Build separate MBG and Riverton income statements, balance sheets, cash views, WIP schedules, and scorecards. Then present a group view with intercompany eliminations. The real reciprocal MBG 89010/Riverton 89011 balance of $850,000.00 is internal and eliminated in consolidation; trade AP 211 to third parties remains.

Do not compare dollar totals without scale and mix. Common-size statements, per-unit metrics, margin, turnover, and risk indicators can improve comparability. A developer with long-duration WIP should not be judged by the same short-cycle metrics as a service unit without adjustment.

Segment profit and allocations

Define segment margin layers:

  • Revenue less traceable variable/direct cost = contribution.
  • Less traceable fixed cost = segment margin.
  • Less allocated common cost = reported segment profit.

Common fixed costs that continue if a segment closes are not relevant to a keep/drop decision merely because allocated. Allocations remain necessary for full reporting and pricing in some contexts, but decision reports should distinguish traceable and allocated amounts.

Assume an illustrative segment has $1,500,000 revenue, $900,000 variable cost, $300,000 traceable fixed cost, and $200,000 allocated common cost. Contribution is $600,000, segment margin $300,000, and reported profit $100,000. Dropping it would not save the $200,000 common cost if that cost continues; group profit would fall $300,000 before other effects.

Entity-specific dashboard controls

Every dashboard row should retain entity, period, source, definition, and last refresh. Reconcile financial KPIs to exact ledgers and WIP schedules. Use role-based access so one entity's sensitive data is not improperly exposed. Preserve versions used in management decisions.

MBG uses bank 102.1 while Riverton uses 102. Group cash must identify restrictions and intercompany movements. Never use a consolidated total to authorize an entity payment without legal availability.

Use exception narratives with owner, cause, impact, action, and deadline. Red/amber/green status needs quantitative thresholds and cannot replace commentary for material items.

Behavior and incentives

Tying compensation to a single measure encourages gaming. Margin-only incentives can delay loss recognition; revenue targets can encourage poor contracts; cash targets can delay valid vendor payments; schedule targets can sacrifice quality. Use balanced measures, multi-period evaluation, clawbacks where appropriate, and independent data controls.

Targets must align with authority. Entity leaders can own controllable working capital and forecast quality; corporate treasury owns facility structure; finance owns definitions and reconciliation; operations owns project evidence. Shared accountability needs explicit decision rights.

Causal map and dashboard review

Build a causal chain explicitly. An illustrative initiative to cross-train project accountants should increase coverage of key reconciliations; that should reduce close delays and unresolved variances; faster reliable information should improve billing and cost decisions; those should improve cash and margin. Assign measures at each link. If training completion rises but reconciliation quality does not, investigate training design or staffing rather than assuming financial benefit.

Targets need baselines and time horizons. Improving on-time cost-to-complete updates from 70% to 95% over six months is different from declaring a permanent 100% target without capacity. Use control limits and trend where process variation matters. One red month may be noise; a sustained shift may require action.

Segment reconciliation

Create a bridge from segment results to entity totals and from entities to consolidated results. The bridge should show unallocated corporate items, intersegment transactions, eliminations, and accounting-policy differences. Segment revenue plus corporate/unallocated and elimination adjustments must equal consolidated revenue; the same discipline applies to profit and assets.

Assume illustratively MBG segment revenue $5,000,000, Riverton $4,000,000, and $600,000 internal revenue from MBG to Riverton. Summed entity revenue is $9,000,000, but consolidated external revenue is $8,400,000 after eliminating the internal $600,000. The elimination does not change each entity's legal ledger.

Review measure quality. Reconcile financial measures to controlled sources; validate nonfinancial populations; retain calculation versions; and test manual adjustments. Dashboard access should be appropriate, but transparency of definitions should not depend on privileged tribal knowledge.

During management review, focus on exceptions, cause, forecast impact, and action. Do not spend the meeting reading every green metric. Confirm that favorable results are complete and sustainable, especially when they conflict with cash, WIP, safety, or customer evidence.

Worked example — the reportable-segment quantitative thresholds

External segment reporting has three quantitative tests, and an operating segment is reportable if it meets any one of them. Assume the following illustrative operating segments.

Operating segmentRevenueProfit (loss)Assets
Residential Construction$5,000,000$400,000$3,200,000
Land Development$4,000,000$(250,000)$4,400,000
Equipment Services$900,000$80,000$700,000
Property Management$600,000$60,000$400,000
Design Studio$300,000$(30,000)$300,000
Combined$10,800,000—$9,000,000

Revenue test. The threshold is 10% of combined revenue: $10,800,000 × 10% = $1,080,000. Residential Construction and Land Development pass; the other three do not.

Profit or loss test. The benchmark is the greater, in absolute terms, of the combined profit of all segments reporting a profit and the combined loss of all segments reporting a loss. Profitable segments total $400,000 + $80,000 + $60,000 = $540,000. Loss segments total $250,000 + $30,000 = $280,000. The benchmark is $540,000 and the threshold is $54,000. Residential Construction ($400,000), Land Development ($250,000), Equipment Services ($80,000) and Property Management ($60,000) all pass; Design Studio's $30,000 does not.

Asset test. The threshold is $9,000,000 × 10% = $900,000. Only Residential Construction and Land Development pass.

Four segments are reportable. Their external revenue is $5,000,000 + $4,000,000 + $900,000 + $600,000 = $10,500,000, which is $10,500,000 ÷ $10,800,000 = 97.22% of consolidated revenue — comfortably above the 75% floor, so no additional segment must be added. Design Studio is aggregated into an "all other" category and reconciled to the consolidated totals.

Trap — netting the profit and loss benchmarks

Trap: the profit-or-loss benchmark is the greater of the two absolute sums, not their net. Netting them gives $540,000 − $280,000 = $260,000 and a threshold of $26,000, which would make Design Studio's $30,000 loss reportable in error and add a segment the standard does not require. The test deliberately uses the larger population so that a group with offsetting profits and losses does not end up with an artificially low threshold.

Trap — the 75% test is a floor, not a result

Trap: the 75% test is applied after the three 10% tests and can force additional segments into reportable status. Had the reportable segments here totalled only 68% of consolidated revenue, more segments would be added — smallest first is not required, but the total must clear 75%. A candidate who stops after the three quantitative tests will get a correct segment list only by luck.

Worked example — keep or drop, with the avoidability question answered properly

Take the illustrative segment with $1,500,000 of revenue, $900,000 of variable cost, $300,000 of traceable fixed cost, and $200,000 of allocated common cost. Contribution is $600,000, segment margin is $300,000, and reported profit is $100,000.

If all $300,000 of traceable fixed cost is avoidable, dropping the segment forfeits $600,000 of contribution and saves $300,000, so group operating income falls by $300,000. The $200,000 of allocated common cost is not saved and is not part of the calculation.

If only $220,000 is avoidable because an $80,000 equipment lease runs three more years, dropping the segment forfeits $600,000 and saves $220,000, so income falls by $380,000 — the earlier answer plus the $80,000 of stranded lease cost.

There is a second-order effect that generates most of the argument in the room. The $200,000 of common cost does not disappear; it is reallocated to the remaining segments, whose reported profits fall by $200,000 in total. Group profit is unchanged by that reallocation, but every surviving segment manager sees a deterioration caused entirely by a decision elsewhere. Report the allocation change explicitly so the reallocation is not mistaken for performance.

Trap — reported segment profit is not the decision number

Trap: the segment shows $100,000 of reported profit, so dropping it looks like it would cost $100,000. The real cost is $300,000, or $380,000 with the unavoidable lease. Reported profit is contaminated by $200,000 of unavoidable allocation. The relevant figure is contribution less avoidable fixed cost, and the only way to identify that is to test each fixed cost for avoidability rather than reading the traceable-cost line.

Worked example — reconciling segments to consolidated results

Segment disclosure requires a reconciliation to consolidated amounts, and the reconciliation is where entity discipline becomes visible.

Revenue reconciliationAmount
MBG segment revenue$5,000,000
Riverton segment revenue$4,000,000
Total reportable segment revenue$9,000,000
Less intersegment revenue, MBG to Riverton$(600,000)
Consolidated external revenue$8,400,000
Profit reconciliationAmount
MBG segment profit$620,000
Riverton segment profit$310,000
Total reportable segment profit$930,000
Unallocated corporate expense$(340,000)
Elimination of unrealized intercompany profit$(45,000)
Consolidated pre-tax income$545,000

Both bridges expose what a summed dashboard hides. The $600,000 of internal revenue is real to each entity's legal ledger and unreal to the group. The $45,000 of unrealized profit sits inside an asset one entity still holds and must come out of consolidated income even though neither entity's own statements are wrong.

Trap — adding entity columns to get a group total

Trap: $5,000,000 plus $4,000,000 is not $9,000,000 of consolidated revenue, and $620,000 plus $310,000 is not $930,000 of consolidated profit. Every dashboard row that shows MBG and Riverton side by side needs a labeled elimination column and a total that ties to the consolidated statements. A "group" total produced by summing entity columns overstates revenue by $600,000 and profit by $385,000 here, and it is the single most common defect in management reporting for a related-party group.

Trap — a scorecard target met through the denominator

Trap: the illustrative 90% on-time milestone result — 18 of 20 — is met, yet two of those on-time milestones were achieved through unapproved scope reductions. The guardrail, an approved and frozen scope baseline, is what converts the ratio from a number into evidence. Any percentage measure can be hit by managing its denominator; every percentage target therefore needs a defined, controlled and reconciled population before it is used in an incentive plan.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests segment profitability, allocations, common-size analysis, scorecard causality, and management interpretation. Questions often ask whether a segment should be dropped or why a metric is misleading. Separate avoidable cost from allocated cost and entity performance from consolidated elimination.

Practice and recap

  1. Map strategy across four balanced-scorecard perspectives.
  2. Pair leading drivers with lagging outcomes and guardrails.
  3. Define segment margin layers and allocation policy.
  4. Prepare entity reports before consolidated views.
  5. Reconcile financial measures and govern nonfinancial sources.
  6. Review incentives for gaming and unintended risk.

Reliable definitions let leaders compare performance without rewarding accounting noise or hidden risk.

Recap: a balanced scorecard measures the system that creates results, while segment reporting shows where results arise. MBG and Riverton can share a dashboard without losing their separate identities or turning internal activity into external performance.

flashcards.front: What are the four balanced-scorecard perspectives?
flashcards.back: Financial, customer/stakeholder, internal process, and learning and growth.
A measure of an activity or capability expected to drive a future outcome.
Segment revenue less variable/direct cost and traceable fixed cost, before allocated common fixed cost.
It may continue if a segment closes and therefore may be irrelevant to a keep/drop decision.

flashcards.front: What are the MBG and Riverton GL totals?
Can a group dashboard combine entity cash for payment authorization?
flashcards.back: No. Legal availability, restrictions, and bank/entity boundaries must be preserved.
A companion condition that prevents a target from being achieved through harmful or invalid behavior.
They reduce gaming and balance short-term financial outcomes with customers, processes, capability, and risk.

questions.q: Which is a leading indicator of project margin quality?
questions.explain: Estimate discipline is a process driver that can reveal margin change before final outcomes.

questions.q: Illustratively, 18 of 20 milestones are on time. Rate is:
Segment revenue $1.5M, variable cost $0.9M, traceable fixed cost $0.3M. Segment margin is:
Allocated common cost is $200,000 and continues if segment closes. For keep/drop, it is generally:
choices: Unavoidable and not a benefit of dropping
questions.explain: A continuing common cost is not saved by dropping the segment.

questions.q: What happens to valid MBG/Riverton reciprocal balances in consolidated reporting?
questions.explain: The group cannot report internal receivables/payables against itself.

questions.q: Which incentive creates likely dysfunctional behavior?
choices: Margin-only bonus that rewards delayed loss recognition
questions.explain: A single margin target can motivate optimistic estimates and delayed recognition.

questions.q: Why can MBG and Riverton appear side by side but not be silently combined?
choices: They are distinct legal entities with separate banks, ledgers, and obligations
questions.explain: Group reporting must preserve entity facts and show explicit consolidation eliminations.
